text: Question seven. Sessions versus JWT versus oh-auth, how do they relate? They answer different questions. With a session, the server stores the login and hands the client an opaque ID, usually in a cookie: forty-three random characters that mean nothing without the server's store. JWT, a jay-son Web Token, is a signed format for claims. This one is a hundred sixty-four characters, and anyone can read it: decode the middle part, and there's the user, the role, and the expiry. The signature proves who issued it: change the role to admin, and it no longer verifies. Oh-auth isn't a token format at all. It's a framework for delegated authorization: letting one app reach your data on another service without your password. Its access tokens may be JWTs or opaque strings. Question eight. When would you choose stateful sessions over stateless JWTs? When you need instant revocation, to log a user out or ban them now, and can afford a session store every server shares. Delete the session, and the next request fails. Checked locally, a JWT stays valid until it expires, unless every check does a lookup again. JWTs fit many services verifying requests without asking a session store each time. The common hybrid pairs a short-lived access token, say fifteen minutes, with a longer-lived refresh token that can be revoked. A banned user then keeps access for at most those fifteen minutes.
